references.text: Joseph threw himself on his father Jacob's neck and wept. The expression 'threw himself on his neck' (ἐπέπεσεν ἐπὶ τὸν τράχηλον) is used in a similar way in [ref:Gen 46:29|Genesis 46:29], where a father and son are reunited after a long separation.

Esau ran to meet his brother Jacob, embraced him, threw himself on his neck and kissed him – a close parallel to the father's reaction in [ref:Gen 33:4|Genesis 33:4], with the same combination of running, throwing oneself on the neck and kissing.

Joseph threw himself on his brother Benjamin's neck and wept, and kissed all his brothers ([ref:Gen 45:14-15|Genesis 45:14-15]). The reunion scene has strong parallels to the return of the prodigal son.

The context for the parable: tax collectors and sinners came to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes grumbled ([ref:Luke 15:1-2|Luke 15:1-2]). The father's loving reception of the prodigal son illustrates God's acceptance of sinners.
The prodigal son decided to get up and go to his father ([ref:Luke 15:17-19|Luke 15:17-19]). Verse 20 shows the fulfillment of this decision – he got up (ἀναστὰς) and came to his father.

Peter's words that the promise applies to 'all who are far away' ([ref:Acts 2:39|Acts 2:39]) provide a theological parallel to the father seeing the son while he is still far off (μακρὰν ἀπέχοντος), and God's initiative to reach those who are distant.

Paul writes that those who were once far away have been brought near by Christ's blood ([ref:Eph 2:13|Ephesians 2:13]). The image of being 'far away' and being received mirrors the father's reception of the son who was far off.
The Lord had deep compassion (ἐσπλαγχνίσθη) for the widow in Nain ([ref:Luke 7:13|Luke 7:13]). The same Greek word is used to describe the father's deep compassion when he saw his son coming home.
Jesus had deep compassion (ἐσπλαγχνίσθη) for the crowd ([ref:Mark 6:34|Mark 6:34]). This word for deep, inner compassion is the same as that which describes the father's reaction in the parable.

God says: 'My heart recoils within me; all my compassion is aroused' ([ref:Hos 11:8|Hosea 11:8]). God's love for his unfaithful people is mirrored in the father's deep compassion for the prodigal son.

'Let the wicked forsake his way ... let him turn to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him' ([ref:Isa 55:7|Isaiah 55:7]). The son's return and the father's mercy illustrate this prophetic promise of grace for those who repent.

The parable of the lost sheep ([ref:Luke 15:4-7|Luke 15:4-7]) has the same theme: God's active seeking and joy over what was lost. The father running to meet his son illustrates God's initiative in salvation.
